title: AI campaign deepfakes are starting to draw legal threats
key_facts: Attorneys for Democratic congressional candidate Rebecca Cooke sent a cease-and-desist letter, dated 30 Sep 2026, to Republican Rep. Derrick Van Orden, whom she is challenging in Wisconsin's 3rd district this November.
The letter is about AI-made videos Van Orden posted to X that show Cooke saying things she never said; they carry an automatic 'Grok Imagine' label.
It points to an AI video shared on 4 Aug in which a fake Cooke makes false statements, and calls the content 'pure fiction'.

The letter says Van Orden risks breaking Wisconsin's rule that bars a public figure from defaming someone with 'actual malice', and warns that Cooke's lawyers are weighing 'all legal options' if he continues.
Van Orden's campaign accused Cooke of throwing a 'full blow tantrum'; Van Orden answered on social media with another Grok-assisted video.
Cooke lost to Van Orden by about 3 percentage points in 2024.
quote_evidence: "Ms. Cooke never made the statements attributed to her," attorney Ben Stafford wrote on Sept. 30.

The letter says that Cooke's attorneys are monitoring Van Orden's social media accounts, and warns that they are weighing "all legal options" if Van Orden persists in "misusing AI to defame Ms. Cooke."
why_it_matters_hint: It is an early test of whether older defamation law can be used against AI fakes in a campaign where state election rules are thin.
notes: Axios original returned HTTP 403 (blocked). Wrote from Wisconsin Public Radio's report of the Cooke letter to Van Orden, which is the most likely case behind the Axios headline, but the Axios piece may cover more cases. The Milwaukee Journal Sentinel also reported the letter (headline only seen).
